articles.title: Trump gir Elon Musk prestisjefylt utmerkelse
articles.content:
Teknologimilliardær Elon Musk ble torsdag tildelt National Medal of Science, en av USAs mest prestisjefylte vitenskapelige utmerkelser.

Musk fikk overlevert medaljen av USAs president Donald Trump under en konferanse i Washington torsdag. Trump kalte Musk for en «nasjonalskatt» og «vår tids Thomas Edison» da han overrakte medaljen.

Musk leder romfartsselskapet SpaceX og elbilprodusenten Tesla.

Også toppsjefene fra Google, Nvidia, AMD, Dell og Microsoft fikk tildelt lignende utmerkelser på konferansen.

Musk ledet fram til slutten av mai i fjor effektiviseringsetaten Doge, der han gjennomførte omfattende kutt i kostnader og ansatte i offentlige etater.

Etter å ha kunngjort sin avgang, havnet han og Trump i en offentlig krangel der de fremsatte beskyldninger og påstander mot hverandre.

Etter krangelen ser Musk nå ut til å være tilbake i den amerikanske presidentens innerste krets. USAs forsvarsminister ga nylig Musk en ledende rolle i et prosjekt som skal se på fremtidens krigføring.

Donald Trump

Donald Trump ble innsatt som USAs 47. president 20. januar 2025. Det er hans andre periode som president.

articles.title: Bolsonaro får støtte fra nummer tre i presidentvalget
articles.content:
Den Trump-vennlige presidentkandidaten Flávio Bolsonaro i Brasil har fått støtte fra politikeren som endte på tredjeplass.

Augusto Cury fikk nesten tre prosent av stemmene i første runde av presidentvalget søndag 4. oktober.

Nå har Cury stilt seg bak Bolsonaro, melder nyhetsbyrået AFP.

Bolsonaro endte to prosentpoeng foran Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva i den første valgrunden i presidentvalget. Bolsonaro fikk rundt 47 prosent av stemmene, mens Lula fikk 45 prosent.

– Min støtte er ikke en blankofullmakt, sier Cury imidlertid i en uttalelse.

Støtten fra Cury kan hjelpe Bolsonaro når han skal møte Lula i den andre og siste valgrunden i presidentvalget. Den holdes 25. oktober.

Brasil

President Lula da Silva vant presidentvalget i Brasil i oktober og ble innsatt 1. januar 2023. 8. januar gikk støttespillere av tidligere president Jair Bolsonaro til angrep på Kongressen, presidentpalasset og høyesterett i hoevdstaden Brasília.

                        State-run workplaces in Norway will need to recruit more staff with an immigrant background, Norway’s Royals resume official programme and more news on Thursday.

The Nobel Peace Prize 2026 to be announced on Friday

The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 will be announced at a press conference on Friday, October 9th at 11am at the Norwegian Nobel Institute in Oslo.

This year, 287 individuals and organisations have been nominated, though the names on the list are kept secret for 50 years.

As the name of last year’s Peace Prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, was apparently leaked the night before the official event, strict steps are being taken this year to prevent any leaks ahead of the announcement.

“We are doing many things to prevent this from happening again, but we cannot say much about the details, because then we would make ourselves vulnerable again. But a lot of resources have been spent on measures,” Kristian Berg Harpviken, Director of the Norwegian Nobel Institute, told news agency NTB.

Along with the security measures, the Norwegian Nobel Committee knows it will be under a lot of scrutiny and political attention.

Just days before the prize is announced in Oslo, US President Donald Trump, who was also nominated in 2025, said he deserves the award.

According to news agency AFP, even though he has not been lobbying as openly for the Nobel in recent weeks, Trump remains on everyone's minds, with strong chances that the committee's pick will, regardless of who they choose, be interpreted as direct or indirect criticism of the US president.

Trump is "the spectre in the room", said the head of the Peace Research Institute in Oslo (PRIO), Haakon Gjerløw.

"There's always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee. So in one sense we're very used to that,"  Harpviken told AFP.

You can watch the announcement live on the Nobel Peace Prize website.

Norwegian vocabulary: Nobels fredspris - Nobel Peace Prize

State workplaces to face new diversity requirements from 2027

Norway’s government will introduce new diversity guidelines for public sector workplaces, including ministries, directorates and state agencies, as reported by multicultural newspaper Utrop.

A new circular from the Ministry of Digitalisation said the main goal is to increase the hiring of employees with an immigrant background. "The business should have a positive development in the proportion of employees with an immigrant background," the circular said.

​The new guidelines are set to take effect from 2027 and will be in place for three years, until 2029.

The authorities pointed out, among other things, that employees from different backgrounds can be a valuable resource when state institutions work with diverse groups across the population, as well as providing access to broader expertise.

The requirement covers both first-generation immigrants and people born in Norway to foreign parents.

State agencies must set diversity targets and report their progress each year until 2029. However, strict privacy rules will remain in place. This means that employers can't ask for sensitive information like national origin, religion, or ethnicity during the hiring process or after the person has been hired.

Norwegian vocabulary: innvandrerbakgrunn - immigrant background

Norway’s Royal House resumes official programme after period of court mourning

On Wednesday, the Royal House released several statements about the royal family, sharing key updates for the coming months.

King Haakon will visit Narvik on Tuesday, October 13th, marking the first official municipal visit as Norway’s new king.

Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra will keep focusing on her studies and plans to return to Australia in February. This semester, she is on exchange at the University of Oslo and will participate in some official events until next year.

Finally, Queen Mette-Marit will not take part in any official events until next summer. “Her Majesty the Queen is still in rehabilitation after the lung transplant and will initially have no official programme until next summer,” the Royal House confirmed in a press release.

On Wednesday, the government presented its draft state budget for 2027, setting out its spending priorities for the coming year and kicking off a period of intense political negotiations.

The proposal includes major changes in several areas, such as taxes, family support, electric vehicle incentives, energy subsidies, public transport and big investments in national security and defence.

The announcement has received mixed reactions. Some sectors welcome the targeted economic support, but opposition parties have already expressed strong disagreements with key parts of the proposal.

The budget will now be debated among political parties who will negotiate potential adjustments before the final version is officially approved in December.

In the next few days, we will publish detailed articles about the Norwegian economy and how these decisions might affect the international community living in Norway.

                        The Norwegian government said Wednesday it plans to increase funding for the country's foreign intelligence services to step up surveillance of neighbouring Russia.

In a 2027 budget bill, the Labour government proposed a funding boost of some 400 million kroner (37.3 million euros), without specifying the total budget.

"We must understand the developments around us quickly, correctly and precisely," said Defence Minister Tore Sandvik.

"It is important that Etterretningstjenesten (the intelligence services) and the armed forces have a robust and continuous capacity to assess threats in areas of interest to Norway and to sound the alarm," Sandvik added, quoted in a press release.

Norway shares a 198-kilometre (125 miles) land border with Russia in the Arctic and often describes itself as NATO’s "eyes and ears" in Europe's far north.

The country is geographically close to the Kola Peninsula, where Russia stations much of its nuclear arsenal.

A further budget proposal also calls for a 250 million kroner increase in funding for the domestic intelligence service, PST.

According to finance minister and former NATO secretary general, Jens Stoltenberg, Oslo plans to allocate 3.4 percent of its GDP to defence in 2027, commensurate with the 3.5 percent target for 2035 which NATO member countries have agreed.

As Norway has a minority government, the proposal for more cash will require the support of several parties to pass the bill, which is therefore likely to undergo amendments.

articles.title: Maricarmen (87) som utløste spanske boligprotester er død
articles.content:
Det melder leietakerforeningen i Madrid i en uttalelse.

Foreningen har støttet 87-åringens kamp for å få bli boende i leiligheten hun hadde hatt hele livet. Nye eiere hevet husleien kraftig. Abascal kunne ikke betale den nye leien, og ble til slutt kastet ut 24. september.

Utkastelsen av pensjonisten ble et sterkt symbol og utløste massive demonstrasjoner i den spanske hovedstaden. Under én uke etter utkastelse, fikk hun tilbudet om å flytte hjem igjen – noe hun sa ja til.

articles.title: 'The world’s loneliest place': Norway ranked the 'hardest country to make friends'
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        It’s official: Norway has been ranked as the hardest country in the world for international residents to settle in and build a social life, according to a major global survey. But does this really come as a surprise?

Norway landed at the bottom of the rankings in the latest InterNations survey, which is based on responses from thousands of foreign citizens living around the world.

“Norway finishes 31st out of 31 destinations in 2026. Expats there are the unhappiest in the survey,” the report said, adding that Norway is "the world’s loneliest place".

Whilst the country scored well in the category of Environment and Climate, it was ranked dead last for Ease of Settling In.

This category considered how friendly the locals were in general, how easy it was to make friends with them and whether foreigners find it easy to feel at home in the country.

A significant 72 percent of respondents said making local friends is difficult, which is over 30 percentage points higher than the global average of 40 percent.

"It’s telling that around half (51 percent) describe their friends and acquaintances as mostly other expats (vs 37 percent globally)," the report said, adding that only a quarter (25 percent) are content with their social life in the country (vs 54 percent globally).

READ MORE: Five tips to help you make more friends and combat loneliness in Norway

Fewer than two in five foreigners living in Norway find the local population friendly in general (37 percent vs 63 percent globally) and towards foreign residents specifically (37 percent vs 61 percent).

This lack of social integration and the difficulties it creates, combined with other factors like limited job openings, brutal costs, and a feeling of "having little to do" leaves many foreign residents feeling unhappy with their life.

Less than half of respondents (46 percent) are content with life in Norway, which is much lower than the 70 percent global average.

READ ALSO: Five places to find a sense of community in Norway

When asked if they feel at home in the country, only 31 percent said that they do, compared to 61 percent globally. "Expats feel neither at home nor welcome in Norway," the report concluded.

The struggle for foreign residents to settle in and make friends in Norway is nothing new, the country has been ranked in the bottom 10 for Ease of Settling In for the seventh year in a row.

"I dislike the cost and difficulty of making friends. It’s a lonely country to live in," said a British resident living in Bærum, quoted in the report.

So is it that hard to make friends with locals in Norway? Share your experiences in the comments below.

articles.title: Five tips to help you make more friends and combat loneliness in Norway
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Norway has earned a reputation of a difficult place to settle and make friends over the years. The Local has put together a guide on essential resources to help you fight loneliness.

Meeting new people can certainly feel daunting, and striking up a meaningful connection can be difficult, given the social rules of engagement in Norway.

People tend to be more reserved, and this is generally more out of respect for your privacy than an unwillingness to be social.

Being in an environment that emphasises being social and meeting new people can help take the pressure off completely.

Norway's big cities are home to plenty of networking groups where people can connect, and hopefully form friendships.

Unlock Norway hosts regular events looking to bring Norway's international community together.

Mer av Oslo also runs regular events, such as cooking courses, where you can meet Oslo's locals. However, these events will consist mainly of locals, so a lot of the conversation will likely be in Norwegian.

A go-to for anyone new to Norway should be to join a social media group of other foreign residents. The group could be open to all foreign residents or just those from a specific country.

You can introduce yourself to these groups and explain a bit about your situation. Whether it's a culture clash, feeling homesick, having trouble making friends, or problems connecting with your colleagues, other members in these groups can offer valuable and meaningful insights. They may also be in a similar situation and want to meet up to talk about it.

Being a member of a group of nationals from the same country as you may also help you retain a bit of personal identity so you don't feel so lost living overseas.

Some of these groups may also schedule regular meetups where you can go along and be with other people – alternatively, you could take the initiative yourself.

Picking up a new hobby or getting back into an old interest

Learning something new with other people could help make you feel part of a wider group and allow you to make friends with people outside of the activity.

There are groups for pretty much everything in Norway, so all you need to do is look. Again, social media and your personal network can also help you find people with similar interests and point you toward where to pursue your hobbies.

Having the same mutual interest as someone makes it much easier to strike up a conversation.

Volunteering could be another solution, as spending your free time helping others can be rewarding in more ways than one.

Getting involved could help you to establish friendships with others who may be in a similar situation.

While pretty much everyone in Norway has a good grasp of English, you may not be able to feel fully settled until you've gotten comfortable with Norwegian.

Being unable to communicate in the local language can sometimes make it feel as if you don't have a voice and may put you off trying to find activities and groups to socialise IN.

One overlooked benefit of language courses is the opportunity to meet other people. While online courses are cheaper and more flexible, it may be worth paying the extra money for an in-person course.

Should you want to hone your Norwegian skills outside of the course, then there are plenty of language cafes in Norway's big cities.

One of the benefits of a språkkafe is the more informal setting—and the fact that there's also a cultural exchange element, as people may be interested in the language you speak (if you speak a language other than English).

READ ALSO: Do Norway's 'språkkafé' language cafés actually work?

Getting active is key to making new friends. You can attend networking events or do volunteer work — for example, many foreign residents have built strong social circles by volunteering with local Norwegian organisations (such as Røde Kors or Caritas).

Attending networking events can also be a major bonus, as it allows you to make friends, expand your circle, and even build valuable contacts for the job market.

Sometimes, loneliness can be a symptom of a larger problem, and getting out and meeting people may prove much easier said than done if you find yourself in a mental rut.

If you feel like loneliness is affecting your mental health or that your mental health is making you feel detached from others, then you may wish to access help.

In Norway, mental health help can be accessed both privately and through the state. GPs in Norway can offer treatment for mild or moderate health problems and refer you to a specialist. The GP will contact the mental health services in your area on your behalf.

Those with more acute problems can also access urgent mental healthcare.

articles.content:
Helsestyresmaktene i Pennsylvania melder måndag om over 1000 meslingtilfelle i delstaten, melder Reuters.

198 personar er lagde inn på sjukehus på grunn av sjukdommen.

Også i nabostaten New York er det registrert 108 tilfelle av barnesjukdommen, som det finst vaksinar mot.

Guvernør i New York, Kathy Hochul, har innført smitteverntiltak som skal gjelde fram til 4. november, melder nyheitsbyrået.

Utbrota kjem etter aukande vaksineskepsis i USA på grunn av makta og innverknaden til helseminister Robert F. Kennedy jr., skriv The Guardian.

USA

Fra 20. januar 2025 er Donald Trump igjen president i USA, hvor det bor mer enn 330 millioner mennesker fordelt på 50 stater.

Meslinger

142.000 mennesker døde av meslinger i verden i 2018. Det er 15 prosent flere enn året før, ifølge WHO. Folkehelseinstituttet opplyser at antall tilfeller av meslinger i Norge øker, fra null i 2016, til 12 smittetilfeller i fjor.

Vaksine

De fleste vaksineringer i Norge gis gjennom vaksinasjonsprogrammet for barn og ungdom. Å ta vaksine mot smittsomme sykdommer er ikke påbud i Norge, men mange tar til orde for at det bør bli obligatorisk av hensyn til folkehelsa.

articles.title: 'Opportunities for all': What King Harald’s speech said about integration in Norway
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        As we enter the final months of the year, the government and the King have laid out their political roadmap for 2027. In the King's "Speech from the Throne", the message about immigration and integration was direct and firm.

​King Harald V gave the annual Speech from the Throne (Trontalen) on Friday, October 2nd, officially opening the 171st session of the Norwegian Parliament.

Written by the government to outline its main legislative priorities for the coming year, the speech opened with "Norway is to be a safe country with opportunities for all."

READ ALSO: What’s on the political agenda in Norway this autumn?

The address framed integration policy directly around employment, social participation, and stricter language requirements.

It linked integration to the government's goal of bringing 150,000 more people into the workforce by 2030, which marks a stricter approach to supporting and integrating newcomers.

The speech explicitly said: “People who come to Norway to settle are to be met with clearer demands and expectations as regards learning Norwegian, participating in society and finding work.”

This aligns directly with the government's commitment to the "work line" policy, emphasising that state integration programmes and social support will remain strictly tied to active efforts to learn Norwegian and find work.

By including foreign residents in Norway's plan to address labour shortages, the speech also showed a clear focus on helping newcomers join the workforce quickly instead of depending on long-term state support. This suggests that policy changes may come in the future.

Besides integration, the speech also covered other important national priorities.

The government described the current international situation as the most serious security challenge since World War II. It promised economic policies to support households and families, improve housing affordability, set clearer digital rules for young people, and reform the healthcare system.

Fører er en mann i 80-årene som fikk tilsyn av ambulansepersonell. Elgen ble avlivet.
